figures.caption: Figure 2: NeuroMotion architecture. EEG segments are encoded into continuous representations trained to align with discrete motion primitives learned by a VQ tokenizer. The E2M Transformer predicts motion-code sequences from these representations, and the motion decoder reconstructs continuous trajectories from the selected code vectors.

Table 1: Comparison with adapted EEG-to-motion baselines under the last-session test protocol. Values are cohort mean ± between-subject standard deviation. FBM PCC/R2/RMSE evaluate 30-D end-effector positions; FID and Diversity use full 263-D motion. GT denotes real-motion diversity. Diversity is reported without ranking and interpreted relative to GT. Parameters (M) below method names follow FBM/FR/TM order. Subject-level results and paired tests are reported in Appendix D.7.

Figure 3: Comparison on TM (left hip z-axis angle) and FR (X-axis wrist acceleration). The top and bottom panels show representative 40-frame test windows from TM S07 and FR S05, respectively, both from held-out session 03. Black and blue curves denote ground truth and our predictions, respectively; the remaining curves show baseline predictions.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on FBM. We visualize decoded full-body motion from NeuroMotion and representative baselines against the ground truth. Compared with baselines that often produce over-smoothed or disordered poses, NeuroMotion better preserves the locomotion pattern, articulated body structure, and overall motion coherence.

Figure 5: Token-level RSA on FBM S10 (session 11) and FR S05 (session 03). Blue curves show EEG–motion RSA using pre-quantized motion latents. The other curves show ceiling estimates and permutation-based chance controls. Shaded bands indicate 95% confidence intervals for the motion ceiling and both chance baselines.

Figure 6: Token-level t-SNE visualization of EEG embeddings on FBM S10 (session 11) and FR S05 (session 03). Each point represents an EEG token, colored by the code ID assigned to its paired ground-truth motion token. The four most frequent motion codes in each test session are shown. Code IDs refer to the respective dataset-specific motion codebook.

Table 4: Codebook capacity on three subjects per dataset: FBM (S02/S07/S10), TM (S02/S06/S07), and FR (S05/S07/S22). Entries are mean ± between-subject standard deviation. The default sizes are K = 32/16/12 for FBM/TM/FR.

Table 5: Model-capacity configurations used in the size ablation. LEEG and LE2M denote the numbers of EEG-encoder and total E2M Transformer layers, respectively. Parameters (M) use the full-model scope specified in Table 1.

Table 7: Temporal token granularity on the same three-subject subsets as Table 4. All stages are retrained. Each 2-s window contains 40 motion frames; Nm = 20/10/5 corresponds to 2×/4×/8× compression. Entries are mean ± between-subject standard deviation.
Table 8: Joint alignment-weight sensitivity on the same three-subject subsets as Table 4, with λpcl = λsupcon = λ and all other settings fixed. Entries are mean ± between-subject standard deviation.

Table 11: Artifact-processing comparison on matched subjects: FBM S02/S07/S10, FR S05/S07/S22, and TM S01/S02/S05. Entries are mean ± between-subject standard deviation over three subjects. Original and processed settings use the same motion targets, splits, and evaluation metrics.

Figure 7: Frequency-band analysis on FBM. We report decoding performance under different EEG frequency-band settings, using PCC (higher is better) and RMSE (lower is better). Results for four FBM subjects (S10/S09/S06/S03) are summarized in a single panel, showing that low-frequency bands generally provide stronger decoding performance than higher-frequency bands.

Figure 8: Token-level RSA alignment analysis on FBM and FR. Each curve shows the RSA score over the motion-token timeline, computed between EEG representations and motion-token representations. We visualize results for four FBM subjects (S03, S06, S09, S10) and four FR subjects (sub-05, sub-07, sub-13, sub-22).

Figure 9: Trajectory distribution visualization using t-SNE on three representative subjects: FBM S10, FR S05, and TM S07. For each dataset, we compare the distributions of ground-truth trajectories, NeuroMotion predictions, and baseline predictions in a shared two-dimensional embedding space. NeuroMotion generally shows stronger overlap with the ground-truth distribution than the baselines.
Figure 10: Decoded poses of eight representative FBM motion-code entries. Each panel shows the second frame obtained by decoding one code in isolation.

Table 12: Full subject-level reconstruction results on FBM. PCC, R2, and RMSE are reported in three vertically stacked panels. Bold and underlined values denote the best and second-best results, respectively, determined using the original unrounded values.

Table 13: Full subject-level distributional results on FBM. Each entry reports FID/Diversity. Lower FID is better; Diversity is reported without ranking because it is interpreted relative to the real-motion reference.
Table 18: EEG encoder architecture. C denotes the number of EEG channels, Ne denotes the number of EEG tokens, and de denotes the EEG embedding dimension. These values are dataset-dependent.

Table 20: E2M Transformer architecture used for parallel motion-token decoding. Ne denotes the number of EEG tokens, Nm denotes the number of motion-token slots, de denotes the EEG encoder output dimension, dm denotes the E2M hidden dimension, and K denotes the motion codebook size. In our implementation, Nm is matched to Ne.
